segments.say: At the end of chapter twelve, the woman in Hana's book opened the letter, read the first line, and went pale. And then the chapter ended. Of course it did. Hana knew, in a vague way, that the author was doing this on purpose. She turned the page anyway. Why does that little trick work so well, even on a tired, sensible person who knows it's a trick?

In 1994, the economist and psychologist George Loewenstein, at Carnegie Mellon University, published a review of curiosity research that has been influential ever since. He proposed what he called the information gap theory. Curiosity, he suggested, arises when we notice a gap between what we know and what we want to know.

Crucially, Loewenstein argued that this gap isn't just interesting. It can feel almost uncomfortable, like an itch. A kind of mild deprivation. And the natural response to an itch is to scratch it. A story that ends a chapter on an unopened letter has created a gap, right there in Hana's mind, and the only way to close it is to turn the page.

show.text: Curiosity arises when attention becomes focused on a gap in one's knowledge.

segments.say: Loewenstein also suggested that curiosity tends to grow when we already know a little about something. If you know nothing at all, the gap doesn't feel important. But once you're invested, once you know the character and her troubles, the missing piece stands out. That's partly why the first chapters of a book can feel slow, and the last chapters can feel impossible to put down.

In 2009, a team led by Min Jeong Kang, at the California Institute of Technology, looked at curiosity inside the brain. People read trivia questions in a scanner, and rated how curious they were to learn each answer. When curiosity was high, areas of the brain associated with reward and anticipation became more active, as if the answer were a small treat on the way.

show.what: People read trivia questions and rated their curiosity while their brains were scanned. Higher curiosity went with more activity in reward-related areas, and with better memory for surprising answers later.

segments.say: They also found something useful. When people were very curious about an answer and got it wrong at first, they were more likely to remember the correct answer later. Curiosity seemed to prepare the brain to hold on to what came next. A story that keeps us curious may also be a story we remember.

Now, if suspense and curiosity are what keep us reading, you'd expect spoilers to be a disaster. If someone tells you how a story ends, the gap is closed before you even begin. There's nothing left to wonder about. Surely, that would spoil it. Most people feel very strongly about this. But in 2011, two researchers decided to test it.

Jonathan Leavitt and Nicholas Christenfeld, at the University of California, San Diego, gave students classic short stories by well-known authors. Some were stories with an ironic twist. Some were mysteries. Some were more literary. Some students read each story as it was written. Others read it with a short paragraph at the start that gave away the ending.

show.where: University of California, San Diego, USA
show.what: Students read classic short stories, with ironic twists, mysteries or literary themes, either as written or with a spoiler paragraph first. On average, they liked the spoiled versions slightly more.

segments.say: And the result surprised almost everyone. For all three kinds of story, on average, people enjoyed the spoiled versions slightly more than the unspoiled ones. Even the twist endings. Even the mysteries. Knowing the ending didn't ruin the pleasure. If anything, it seemed to add a little to it.

The researchers suggested a few possible reasons. One is that knowing the ending might make a story easier to follow, and stories that are easier to process tend to feel more pleasant. Another is that, once you know where things are heading, you can notice the craft along the way, the hints and choices that lead there. You read for how, rather than for what.

It's worth adding that this is an average, and the differences were modest. Some people do hate spoilers, and later studies have found that the effect can depend on the person and the kind of story. But the main lesson is still interesting. Suspense isn't the only thing that makes a story enjoyable. Perhaps not even the most important thing.

Think of the stories people return to again and again. Favorite films watched a dozen times. Childhood books read aloud until the pages come loose. Myths and legends told for thousands of years, whose endings everyone already knows. The pleasure isn't in not knowing. The pleasure is in the journey, and in being carried through it again.

So here's what keeps us reading. A gap we want to close. Knowing just enough about the characters to care. A reward-like feeling of anticipation in the brain. And the deeper pleasure of the journey, which can survive even when we know the end.

show.title: What keeps us reading
items: A gap we want to close

segments.say: This gives Hana a gentle way out, if she wants one. She could read the final page now, close the gap, and go to sleep. The research suggests she might not enjoy the book any less tomorrow. Or she could simply stop in the middle of a chapter, rather than at the end of one. Authors place their cliffhangers at the ends. Stopping halfway through avoids the hook altogether.
Hana smiles at the idea of stopping mid-chapter. It feels oddly rebellious. She decides she'll try it. Just this next chapter, then halfway into the one after, and then she'll stop. Probably.

But there's a bigger question hidden in Hana's book. She's spent five chapters inside the mind of a woman who doesn't exist, feeling her worries and guessing her thoughts. Could that kind of practice change how we understand real people? Some researchers have suggested that it might. And the evidence is more interesting, and more complicated, than you might expect.
